title: Wait before pleasure
hook: when a pleasure beckons, pause, and picture both the enjoying and the regret after (Enchiridion 34)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the critic, and the joke that ends the contest. Your line was better than any receipt. Did a criticism come your way, and did you laugh? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

The kitchen is dark except for the open fridge, and the last slice of cake is right there. Or it's the tab with the shopping cart, or the one more episode button counting down from ten. There's a moment, maybe half a second long, between the urge showing up and your hand moving. It's easy to miss that half second entirely. Section thirty-four of the handbook lives entirely inside it, and asks you to stretch it out. Today: wait before pleasure.
screen: `THE OPEN FRIDGE, THE LAST SLICE.` → `HALF A SECOND BEFORE THE HAND MOVES.` → `WAIT BEFORE PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: First, the guard. When the impression of some pleasure arrives, Epictetus says, be careful not to be swept off by it. Let the thing wait for you. Give yourself a little delay. Notice he doesn't say refuse. He says wait. Second, two pictures. In the delay, he says, call to mind two times. The time when you'll be enjoying the pleasure. And the time after, when you've had it, and you're sorry, and you're scolding yourself. Both are real. Look at both. Third, a third picture to set against them: how glad you'll be, and how you'll think well of yourself, if you hold off. Three scenes, and you get to watch all of them before you choose. Fourth, the honest ending. If, after all that, it seems the right time to enjoy the thing, Epictetus allows it. Just take care, he says, that its sweetness and its pull don't overpower you, and remember how much better it is to know you've won that small contest. This isn't a rule against pleasure. It's a rule against being carried. The pleasure that survives the wait is one you've chosen. Stretch the half second into a few minutes, and the one deciding has had time to look at all three pictures.
screen: `LET THE PLEASURE WAIT FOR YOU.` · `PICTURE THE ENJOYING, AND THE REGRET.` · `PICTURE THE GLADNESS OF HOLDING OFF.` · `IF YOU TAKE IT, DON'T BE CARRIED.` · then, large: `WAIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of an urge you know well: a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a drink, a reply typed too fast. Picture it arriving. Now run Epictetus' three pictures, slowly. The enjoying. The after, and how you might feel. And the gladness of having waited. You don't need to decide anything now. Just practice watching all three before your hand moves. The bell holds the time.
Wait before pleasure. Epictetus' advice to let a pleasure wait, picture the enjoying and the regret, and choose instead of being carried. Today's word.
Your line: wait. When one urge shows up today, wait ten minutes before you act on it. Then choose. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism put a short delay between an urge and acting on it, and in that pause picture both the enjoyment and how they'll feel afterward.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut the uncited claim about craving research (urges pass like waves) and the hedonism etymology; the hook no longer repeats day 351's late-night time stamp.

Enchiridion 34 paraphrased: guard against being carried away by the impression of pleasure; let it wait; allow a delay; remember both times, enjoyment and later repentance and self-reproach; set against them the joy and self-approval of abstaining; if it seems a fit time, beware its sweetness and allurement; remember the better consciousness of victory. Confirm.

'People who work with cravings ... an urge rises and falls like a wave' alludes to urge-surfing in addiction treatment (often credited to G. Alan Marlatt); stated generally, no name. Confirm acceptable.
Greek ἡδονή and 'hedonism' etymology: standard; confirm.
